newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tung sets HK polls timetable, US chides China.
newsitem.headline: Tung sets HK polls timetable, US chides China.

text.p: On the eve of Chinese rule, Hong Kong's future chief executive Tung Chee-hwa on Sunday set a timetable for elections and China's President Jiang Zemin pledged to uphold human rights and freedom.
But Washington chided Beijing for its decision to send in 4,000 troops just hours after the handover. Visiting Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said it was not "the best way to start off".
Tung told visiting Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer that elections for a new legislature would be held next May, Downer told reporters.
The shipping magnate chosen by Beijing to bridge the handover after 156 years of British colonial rule had earlier promised a vote within a year. But he had not named the month.
"Mr Tung gave me a guarantee that those elections would take place... and he expected the elections would take place in May of next year," Downer said.

Hong Kong's democratically elected legislative council, Britain's parting political gift to its territory and the focus of bitter Sino-British feuding, will be replaced hours after the midnight Monday (1600 GMT) handover with a provisional legislature appointed by Beijing.
Several of the territory's most popular lawmakers will be out of a job.
Jiang vowed at a ceremony on Sunday in Beijing's Great Hall of the People to implement strictly promises China made under a 1984 agreement handing Hong Kong back to Chinese rule.

"We will firmly uphold the principles of 'one country, two systems' and 'Hong Kong people governing Hong Kong' as well as a high degree of autonomy," the official Xinhua news agency quoted him as saying.
China would "safeguard the Hong Kong residents' rights and freedoms in accordance with the law".
Albright broke with previous caution to lecture Beijing on the importance of sending the right signals to its 6.4 million future subjects.

"I don't think this is the best way to start off," she said of the decision to send People's Liberation Army troops, armoured cars, helicopters and warships sweeping across the border at dawn on Tuesday.
For many Hong Kong residents, armoured cars will arouse painful memories of the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre.
"It's very important for them to offer reassurances to the people of Hong Kong about their way of life," Albright told reporters.
Streets in the Chinese capital were festooned with banners proclaiming "Wash away 100 years of national shame", and a blimp high over the city declared "Celebrate the return of Hong Kong".

A carnival atmosphere was building in Hong Kong, where heir to the British throne Prince Charles handed out a last batch of colonial knighthoods and honours in the gilded ballroom of Government House.
Outgoing Governor Chris Patten, a devout Christian, preached the virtues of making money from the pulpit of Hong Kong's Roman Catholic cathedral on his last Sunday in office.
And workmen began the task of stripping away the insignia and symbols of colonial rule -- starting with the royal coat of arms at the entrance to Britain's former naval base.
British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook vowed to defend London's democratic legacy, and if necessary rally international support to hold Beijing to its promise to hold popular elections.
"The people of Hong Kong have now had a taste of democracy. It must be a prime objective of British policy to make sure that taste does not become a memory," he told reporters.
Earlier, Albright said: "We expect officials in Beijing and Hong Kong to respect the freedoms of Hong Kong people.
"We will closely watch to see if free and fair elections for a new legislature are conducted as promised at an early date."
Patten attacked "demeaning, patronising, mule-headed" arguments against democracy in the territory, whose new leaders have stressed stability ahead of individual freedoms.
He lambasted a "small band of self-appointed good-mouthers who tell the world that Hong Kongers don't care about democracy and civil liberties but only about making money".
In a radio address, Patten said demonstrators who pour into the streets each year to mark the June 4 anniversary of the Tiananmen killings "gave an eloquent answer to that nonsense".
The outgoing governor's crusade for one-man-one-vote in Hong Kong plunged relations between Britain and China into crisis.
As he welcomed individually a series of world leaders attending end-of-empire pageantry and partying, Tung made clear democratic freedoms in Hong Kong would have limits.

He told the British Broadcasting Corporation that peaceful protests would be permitted, but that advocacy of independence for Taiwan and Tibet -- regarded by Beijing as an act of sedition -- would be another matter.
While he said he would not object to his own effigy being burned, he was less forthcoming about whether insults against Chinese leaders would be tolerated.
Pro-democracy activists have been warned against staging a planned protest on the balcony of the legislature building early on Tuesday while Beijing-appointed lawmakers are being sworn in.
Under controversial laws prepared by the new legislature and due to come into force at midnight, police approval will be required for demonstrations.
In New Delhi, the office of Tibet's exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, predicted on Saturday that Hong Kong was doomed to the same fate as Tibet.
Chinese rulers could not be trusted to keep their promises, a statement said. "Human rights and democracy will be the first casualty of reunification with China," it said.

Tight security was in place around a waterfront hotel owned by Hong Kong billionaire Li Ka-shing where Jiang and Prime Minister Li Peng are expected to stay. Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen flew in, and plunged into a meeting with Tung.
Shortly before Charles hands over Hong Kong to Jiang, the Chinese president will hold his first talks with British Prime Minister Tony Blair.
Political rows were forgotten or ignored by Hong Kong residents on Sunday, as a bright sun illuminated the twilight of imperial rule.
It was a harbinger of hope for superstitious Hong Kongers, though weather experts said it could yet rain on the final parades on Monday.
